Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Rohan Mehta is a 26-year-old South Asian American man who works as an editor at a mid-sized publishing house in Chicago. He is married and, until recently, was regarded by colleagues as meticulous and warm. He presented for therapy approximately eight months after an encounter with police that he describes, quietly and with long pauses, as the event that divided his life into a before and an after.

The incident occurred on a winter evening when Rohan was walking home from a late shift. Officers stopped him in an alley shortcut he had used dozens of times. What followed was prolonged: he was pressed face-down against cold concrete, his cheek against pavement that he later estimated was near freezing, his arms wrenched behind his back. A female officer knelt beside him for much of the encounter, speaking in clipped, commanding tones while her partner searched his bag. He was eventually released without charge. The whole episode lasted perhaps twenty minutes. He has not been able to account for those twenty minutes in any straightforward way since.

In the weeks that followed, Rohan noticed that memory of the event did not behave the way he expected memory to behave. It did not recede. When it surfaced — triggered by something as ordinary as stepping outside on a cold morning and feeling the winter air against his face — it arrived with his body already arranged in the posture of that alley: arms drawn inward, shoulders curled, cheek tilted as though pressed against something hard. He would find himself at his desk at work, manuscripts open in front of him, and realise his body had contracted around a memory he had not consciously chosen to revisit. Sometimes the smell came with it — cold concrete and something chemical, like cleaning solvent — arriving uninvited in the middle of an editorial meeting. And when the memory came in its fullest form, what Rohan felt was not fear but grief, a grief so total it surprised him each time, as though he were mourning something he could not yet name.

He began to avoid the cold. In practical terms this meant refusing to step outside without layering so heavily that no air could reach his skin, even in early autumn. His wife, Priya, noticed he had stopped accompanying her on evening walks. At work, the consequences became harder to conceal. Rohan's office is open-plan, and he shares a small conference room with two female colleagues for weekly editorial reviews. After the incident, being alone in that room with either of them — or with any woman he did not know well — produced a vigilance he could not explain or suppress. He began rescheduling those meetings, citing workload, then simply stopped attending some of them. His managing editor flagged his absences in a performance review three months ago, noting a pattern of avoidance that was affecting the team. Rohan said nothing in response because he had no language for what was happening that did not sound, to him, like the language of someone falling apart.

That sense of falling apart had itself become a source of dread. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost logical, that his responses since the incident were evidence of a fundamental inadequacy — that other people would have moved through this, that his inability to do so confirmed something broken at his core. Alongside this sat a flattening of the future: he had stopped making plans with Priya, stopped pitching book projects he had been excited about, stopped imagining his life at thirty or thirty-five. Nothing in the forward direction felt real or reachable. The life he had been building felt like it belonged to someone else.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment two weeks ago when he began to feel unreal mid-conversation with Priya — a dissociative loosening, as though the room were slightly wrong — and he recognised it as the same feeling he had learned to dread, the leading edge of something he could no longer manage alone. He made the appointment the following morning. What he is most afraid of is that nothing will restore the sense that his life contains possibility. What he is most hoping for, though he struggles to say it directly, is to feel like himself again.
